FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define the prevalence of low back pain caused by the sacroiliac joint.
List five key physical examination maneuvers for diagnosing sacroiliac pain.
Identify the role of imaging studies in diagnosing sacroiliac pain.
Identify the threshold for a sacroiliac block relieving pain to predict the surgical outcome of
management of sacroiliac fusion.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Background
Reliable evidence shows that the sacroiliac joint (SIJ) moves and is innervated.



The SIJ should be included in the differential diagnosis for and noted as a common cause of
low back pain (LBP).
Specific physical examination maneuvers can stress the SIJ and can re-create pain.
Local anesthetic injections can relieve pain.
Long fusion to the pelvis may lead to SIJ degeneration.
Multiple research studies have demonstrated substantial clinical benefit in patients who
undergo SIJ fusion.
Overview
The SIJ is a potential pain generator.
Stabilization of the joint may provide clinical relief and prevent pain.

Overview
Back pain is among the most expensive and debilitating medical problems worldwide.
Eighty percent of the population will experience LBP during their lifetime, and chronic
LBP will manifest in 20% of the population. Although many different causes of LBP exist,
pain from the SIJ often is overlooked. The SIJ is a large load-transmitting joint that
connects the spine to the pelvis. Surgeons understand the small movement of the SIJ;
this small amount of motion may lead to joint degeneration and pain. Stabilization of the
SIJ has considerable clinical effect.
Epidemiology
Prevalence of the SIJ as the etiology of LBP

Epidemiology
LBP is very common. Approximately 15% to 30% of LBP is from the SIJ.1-4 LBP is more
common in patients who have undergone lumbosacral fusion.5 L5-S1 fusion increases
stress on the joint by 50% and L4 through S1 fusion increases the stress on the joint by

2/20

168%. The differential diagnosis for buttock or posterior pelvic pain is complex4 (Figure
1).
Figure 1 Three-dimensional illustration of the lower spine, pelvis, and hips show the
differential diagnosis for buttock pain. (Courtesy of Dr. Baronio, Lombardia, Italy.)
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Anatomy of the SIJ
Motion of the SIJ
Innervation of the SIJ
Osteology

Osteology
The SIJ is the largest joint by surface area in the body. The SIJ connects the spine to the
pelvis and provides stable load transmission of the upper body to the lower extremities.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:07 PM
AAOS | Sacroiliac-Mediated Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076
3/20

The SIJ is a complex joint that involves a sinuous surface, synovial portion, and a
ligamentous area.6 The bony anatomy of the SIJ joint is highly variable. The joint typically
is formed by the sacral segments S1, S2, and S3 with the articulating surface typically
differing between sexes, from S1 through S3 in men and from S1-S2 in women.
The top of the sacrum typically is horizontal; however, in some patients, it is upsloped
lateral to medial, which is referred to as a dysmorphic sacrum. Another congenital
anomaly or anatomic variant of the sacrum is known as a transitional vertebra. A
transitional vertebra occurs in patients with partial or complete fusion of the last lumbar
vertebra and the first sacral vertebra. Classification of anatomic variation was described
by Castellvi et al7 in 1984 (Figure 2). This variant may be present in approximately 5% of
patients.8
The motion of the SIJ is limited. It is reported to be 1.1° to 2.2° in nutation and
counternutation (which is analogous to flexion extension), 0.5° to 8.0° in lateral bending,
and 0.8° to 4.0° in axial rotation.9-12
Figure 2 Illustrations show the classification of lumbosacral transitional vertebrae
according to radiomorphologic and clinical relevance with respect to lumbar disk
herniation. (Reproduced with permission from Castellvi AE, Goldstein LA, Chan DP:
Lumbosacral transitional vertebrae and their relationship with lumbar extradural
defects. Spine 1984;9[5]:493-495.)
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076

Nerves
Innervation of the SIJ

Nerves
The innervation of the SIJ is complex and not well agreed upon; however, the SIJ is
innervated. Hilton law13 states that a nerve crossing a joint can innervate that joint.
Therefore, the ventral lumbosacral plexus and the dorsal primary rami of S1 through S4
may potentially innervate the SIJ. Szadek et al14,15 reported the presence of gross nerve
fibers anteriorly and nociceptive fibers within the anterior capsule and the articular
cartilage, and Vilensky et al16 demonstrated the presence of mechanorepotors in the
sacroiliac ligament.
Joints and Ligaments
Anterior capsule
Interosseous ligament

Joints and Ligaments
The SIJ is contained by a fibrous capsule that connects to the articulating edges of the
sacrum and ilium and is lined by a synovial membrane. The articulating surface of the
sacrum is lined by hyaline cartilage, whereas the iliac surface is lined by fibrocartilage.
Loads across the SIJ are substantial.6,12 Stability of the SIJ is a combination of form
(wedge-shaped sacrum along with the sinuous surface) and force closure (provided by
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:07 PM
AAOS | Sacroiliac-Mediated Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076
5/20

muscular contraction). Multiple ligaments help stabilize the SIJ, including the anterior
and posterior sacroiliac ligaments, sacrotuberous ligament, and sacrospinous ligament.
A component of the posterior sacroiliac ligament, the interosseous ligament is the
primary connection between the sacrum and the ilium and prevents anterior and
inferior motion.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Physical Examination

Physical Examination
Physical examination of the SIJ can reliably determine the probability of it being a source
of pain. No single physical examination maneuver can reliably make this determination;
however, a multi-test strategy is highly reliabile17 (Resource 1). The key physical
examination test is the Fortin finger sign; when asked the location of pain, the patient
points to the posterior superior iliac spine. Provocative physical examination tests
include thigh thrust; flexion, abduction, external rotation; pelvic gapping; pelvic
compression; and the Gaenslen test (Figure 3). Occasionally, sacral thrust is included in
this multi-test strategy. In provoking pain in this manner, differentiation of the posterior
hip capsule from the posterior superior iliac spine as the source of pain is important.
Asking the patient if the pain provoked is the typical pain or different pain also is
important. In Europe, the active straight leg raise test also is frequently used.18 Because
simultaneous hip or spine pathology may be present,4 these possible pain generators
also should be examined.

Figure 3 Clinical photographs show provocative physical examination tests. (Courtesy of
David W. Polly, Jr, MD, Minneapolis, MN.)
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
Imaging studies provide poor objective characteristics of SIJ pathology. Radiographs and
CT scans may depict degenerative changes, such as the vacuum phenomenon in the
joint space, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation, which are associated with
a positive correlation for pain originating from the SIJ; however, all imaging studies are
associated with a high false-positive/false-negative ratio.
Radiography
Normal versus dysmorphic sacrum
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:07 PM
AAOS | Sacroiliac-Mediated Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076
7/20


Radiography
Plain radiographs should be the first imaging studies obtained in evaluating the SIJ. The
best views for evaluation of the SIJ are a true AP view and a lateral view of the pelvis.
Morphology of the sacrum can be determined based on plain radiographs. Comparison
between a normal and dysmorphic sacrum is shown in Figure 4.
Figure 4 AP pelvis radiographs. A, Radiograph demonstrates a male pelvis with normal
morphology and a relatively horizontal sacrum. Note articulation of the sacrum at S1
through S3 with the ilium. B, Radiograph demonstrates a dysmorphic and upsloped
sacrum. (Courtesy of David W. Polly, Jr, MD, Minneapolis, MN.)
Computed Tomography
Degenerative changes
Vacuum phenomenon

Computed Tomography
CT is the next imaging modality performed to detect potential pathology because it is
associated with greater sensitivity and provides more detailed information. CT is used
for preoperative planning and to detect degenerative changes, such as joint space
narrowing, cysts, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, and the vacuum phenomenon. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:07 PM
AAOS | Sacroiliac-Mediated Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076
8/20

vacuum phenomenon is the presence of gas within the joint space. The presence of gas
in the joint space is suggestive of joint mobility.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI also can be used to assess for pathology in the area of the sacrum or the SIJ.
Dissimilar from CT scans, MRIs may reveal areas of inflammation and articular erosions,
such as that which may occur in patients with sacroiliitis and ankylosing spondylitis. MRIs
afford much of the anatomic visualization observed on CT scans; however, the patient is
not exposed to radiation during MRI.
Other Tests/Studies
Diagnostic blocks

Other Tests/Studies
Confirmation that the SIJ is the source of pain is achieved via image-guided local
anesthetic injection (Figure 5). Accessing the SIJ may be a challenge; therefore, a
confirmatory arthrography is an important component of injection. The SIJ only holds 1.5
to 2.0 mL. Injection of volumes beyond this limit likely extravagates and makes the pain
response difficult to interpret. To optimize the efficacy of a diagnostic block, pain
medications should be withheld the day of the injection, and patients should be
encouraged to perform the activities that usually flare symptoms so they are sufficiently
symptomatic during the injection. Immediately after the injection, patients are
encouraged to perform the activities that flare symptoms while the local anesthetic is in
effect. This also helps provide clarity. Patients are asked to rate their pain on a visual
analog scale ranging from 0 to 10 before injection and 30 minutes after injection. Some
debate exists with regard to what constitutes a positive response. The International
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:07 PM
AAOS | Sacroiliac-Mediated Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076
9/20

Society for the Advancement of Spine Surgery advocates a 50% reduction, whereas the
North American Spine Society advocates an 80% reduction. Polly et al19 reported no
difference in the surgical response rate between patients with 50% to 75% relief and
those with relief greater than 75%.
Figure 5 Images show image-guided local sacroiliac joint injection. A, Fluoroscopic image
shows considerable extra-articular extravasation. B, Fluoroscopic image shows needle
placement within the joint. C, CT scan shows the needle within the joint. (Courtesy of
David W. Polly, Jr, MD, Minneapolis, MN.)
Diagnosis

Diagnosis
Currently, no definitive diagnostic standard exists for SIJ pain. Pain at or near the
posterior superior iliac spine that can be pointed to with a single finger (Fortin finger
sign), at least three of five positive findings on provocative physical examination
maneuvers, and at least 50% reduction with image-guided SIJ injection of local anesthetic
are used to diagnose the SIJ as the main source of pain.
Differential Diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:07 PM
AAOS | Sacroiliac-Mediated Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076
10/20

Other sources of pain that may mimic SIJ pain should be ruled out. Other potential pain
generators include the hip joint, quadratus lumborum spasm, piriformis syndrome, and
cluneal nerve neuroma (Maingne).
Management
Nonsurgical Management

Nonsurgical Management
Medical management is the first line of treatment for patients with SIJ pain. Although
evidence on the efficacy of nonsurgical management is low, a low level of risk is
associated with nonsurgical management. SIJ-specific physical therapy, NSAIDs, sacroiliac
belts, manual therapy, injections, and radiofrequency ablation typically are used.20
Targeted injections in the sacroiliac region can be used as a diagnostic and therapeutic
intervention and may serve as an adjunct to physical therapy. In patients who have a
positive response to diagnostic blocks but report persistent symptomatic exacerbations
or recurrence, radiofrequency ablation may provide longer lasting therapeutic benefit
(Resource 2).
Surgical Management
Indications

Indications
Although nonsurgical treatment is effective in some patients, it may not be sufficient for
all patients. Surgical treatment may be considered in patients in whom medical
management fails and who have clinically important limitations caused by pain
confirmed to originate from the SIJ (Resource 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:07 PM
AAOS | Sacroiliac-Mediated Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076
11/20

Techniques/Procedures

Techniques/Procedures
Surgical management of SIJ pain has a long history, and multiple techniques have been
described for the surgical management of SIJ pain.21 These include a Smith-Petersen
lateral approach, an anterior sub-iliacus muscle direct anterior approach, and various
direct posterior approaches. These conventional open approaches are associated with
considerable morbidity. Since 2010, minimally invasive approaches have been
advocated, resulting in less morbidity and reasonable efficacy,22 with the lateral-to-
medial trans-iliac approach being one of the most common minimally invasive
approaches.
Surgical Approaches
Although many techniques have been used for joint fusion (Figure 6), minimally invasive
approaches have become popular.
Trans-iliac approach23: The patient is placed in the prone position. Using fluoroscopy or
three-dimensional computer navigation, a Kirschner wire is passed across the ilium and into
the sacrum. Over the guidewire, the soft tissue is dilated, drilled, and broached, and the
implant is placed. Positioning of the implant is assessed via fluoroscopy and/or
intraoperative CT. This process is repeated two more times. Typically, three implants with
good spread and purchase are placed. Two implants are occasionally placed, with four
implants rarely placed; however, the number of implants placed is determined by anatomy.
Ingrowth screw fusion: Various bone ingrowth screws are available and are designed to be
placed in a similar trajectory as triangular titanium rods in the trans-iliac approach. To date,
limited clinical outcomes data are available on this technique.
Screw fixation with decortication: For screw fixation with decortication, trajectory and image
guidance is used. A tube-type device is docked on the ilium. The ilium is drilled, and the bone
is saved. A decortication device is used within the SIJ, and a bone graft is placed. A large
screw followed by a smaller counterrotation screw are placed.
Posterolateral approach: The posterolateral approach comes obliquely through the ilium,
through the interosseous ligament, and into the sacrum. This typically is performed via a

9/3/26, 6:07 PM
AAOS | Sacroiliac-Mediated Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076
12/20

threaded cage with bone graft material.
Figure 6 Axial CT scan of a pelvis shows sacroiliac joint fusion approaches. (Courtesy of David
W. Polly, Jr, MD, Minneapolis, MN.)
Postoperative Management

Postoperative Management
Patients are reevaluated postoperatively for adverse events and discharged home based
on surgeon discretion. Patients adhere to heel-toe, touch-down weight bearing with the
use of a front-wheeled walker or crutches for 3 weeks postoperatively. Weight bearing is
progressively increased until patients are fully ambulatory. In addition, patients are
asked to undergo individualized physical therapy (recommended twice weekly for 1 to 3
weeks postoperatively) as appropriate for their individual needs.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Pitfalls of surgical management include anatomic variations (dysmorphic sacrum), neural canal
impingement, inadequate sacral purchase, poor sacral bone density, and inadequate healing.

13/20

Complications
Wound infection
Wound hematoma and deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism
Allergic reaction to implant
Increased pain at SIJ or surrounding area
Need for additional surgery
Incomplete pain relief
Bleeding
Muscle and/or nerve insult
Loosening failure
Death from medical complication
Nonunion

Nonunion
Determination of failure of the procedure begins with patient-reported outcome
measures showing inadequate improvement. Plain radiography is next. Typically, haloing
is observed on the sacral side of the implant for devices placed in a lateral-to-medial
direction. CT scan can be helpful. Repeat diagnostic injection is critical.
Outcomes

Outcomes
Two randomized controlled trials, two prospective cohort studies, multiple comparative
effectiveness studies, and numerous retrospective cohort studies have compared
minimally invasive surgery with nonsurgical management. Multiple devices have been
approved for use in minimally invasive SIJ fusion. The most-studied devices are triangular
titanium rods placed in a lateral-to-medial approach (two randomized controlled trials,
one prospective cohort study, three comparative effectiveness studies, and numerous
retrospective cohort studies). Published 5-year results from prospective studies on
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:07 PM
AAOS | Sacroiliac-Mediated Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001076
14/20

triangular titanium rods show a low rate of revision surgery. Summary data on clinical
success show that 80% of patients who met entry criteria for the clinical trials (>6
months of failed nonsurgical management, three of five positive physical examination
findings, >50% reduction of pain with image-guided local anesthetic injections, and hip
and spine ruled out as pain generators) experienced a 50% reduction of in Oswestry
Disability Index and visual analog scale scores.
The best data to date comes from two randomized controlled trials involving the use of
bone ongrowth triangular titanium rods.24,25 Both trials showed clinically important
improvement in patients who underwent surgical treatment compared with nonsurgical
treatment. Using the same inclusion criteria technology, a prospective cohort study
involving the use of triangular titanium rods reported that patients who underwent
surgical treatment had marked improvements in pain, disability, and quality of life.26 All
three studies showed clinically meaningful improvement in Oswestry Disability Index and
visual analog scales scores27 (Figure 7). The iFuse Implant System Minimally Invasive
Arthrodesis study also reported improved walking distance and employment status
postoperatively. Many retrospective cohort studies have reported comparable
improvements.

More recently, two prospective cohort studies have been performed with the use of
other technologies. Fuchs and Ruhl28 reported similar improvement via intra-articular
